title: Mithun's Daughter Said Yes. Dishani Chakraborty Is Engaged — and the Proposal Pictures Are Pure Cinema.
excerpt: "The easiest forever I've ever known." Dishani Chakraborty announced her engagement to steadicam operator Myles Mantzaris with a dreamy carousel, and a December 6 wedding is already locked.
body:
It's three slides, and it's a whole love story. First: a man on one knee, the kind of frozen-mid-breath moment every proposal photographer prays for. Second: a hand, a ring, and a smile she clearly couldn't hold in. Third: a kiss. And underneath, a caption with the restraint of someone who doesn't need to oversell it — "06.12.2026… The easiest forever I've ever known."

With that, Dishani Chakraborty — daughter of the legendary Mithun Chakraborty — told the world she's getting married.

The lucky man is Myles Mantzaris, and refreshingly, he's not a star. He's a steadicam operator and colourist — a behind-the-camera craftsman, the sort of person who makes everyone else look luminous and rarely gets photographed himself. There's something quietly lovely about a film family's daughter choosing someone from the technical side of the industry, the people who actually build the magic. The wedding is set for December 6, 2026, and the date is already doing rounds on every Bollywood timeline.

"06.12.2026… The easiest forever I've ever known." — Dishani Chakraborty

The pictures went up on Instagram and did exactly what you'd expect: lit up the comments within minutes. Dishani has always kept a lower profile than the Chakraborty name might allow — no film launches, no manufactured paparazzi moments — so the engagement reveal felt genuinely personal rather than packaged. The proposal images, all soft light and unguarded grins, leaned into romance without tipping into staged. You believe these two.

For those who need the family tree: Dishani is the adopted daughter of Mithun Chakraborty and his wife, former actress Yogeeta Bali, who married in 1979. The couple also have three sons — Mimoh, Ushmey, and Namashi — but Dishani is the only daughter, which makes a December wedding in the Chakraborty household a very big deal indeed.

And the man whose blessing she has? That's not a small thing either. Mithun Chakraborty is one of Indian cinema's most singular figures — a National Award winner straight out of the gate for his 1976 debut Mrigayaa, then a full-blown phenomenon after 1982's Disco Dancer turned him into a dancing icon whose fame stretched from Mumbai to Moscow. Across the decades he's done it all: the gritty action of Agneepath, the populist masala of his eighties run, the late-career gravitas of The Kashmir Files. In January 2026 he was honoured with the Dadasaheb Phalke Award, Indian cinema's highest. Now he's planning a wedding.

For the diaspora, the Chakraborty name carries a particular nostalgia. Disco Dancer was a cultural export before "cultural export" was a phrase anyone used — beloved across the former Soviet bloc, played at desi parties from New Jersey to London for forty years running. NRI households of a certain vintage grew up on "I am a Disco Dancer." So watching the next generation of that family step into her own spotlight, on her own terms, lands as something warmer than ordinary celebrity gossip. It feels like family news.

https://www.instagram.com/p/DZmXWZ7jJhf/

There's a tidy poetry to the match, too. Myles works in colour grading — the unglamorous, painstaking craft of making every frame on screen look exactly as warm or as cold as it needs to feel. Dishani comes from a family that has spent fifty years inside that frame. The bride raised on stories of how the magic gets made, marrying the man who quietly makes it: it's the kind of detail a screenwriter would be told to cut for being too neat.

No word yet on where the December ceremony will be held or how grand the guest list runs — though given Mithun's standing in the industry and his recent political and cinematic profile, expect the who's-who of Bollywood to turn up. Whether the couple opt for an intimate affair or a full-scale destination spectacle remains to be seen. If Mithun's own larger-than-life career is any guide, restraint may not be the operative word.

What we do know: a steadicam operator who spends his life keeping the frame steady just locked down the steadiest thing of all. December 6. Mark it.
